ground_truth_core_content:
Introduction:
**1:** As with the previous generation for this preset, this article splits its introduction across the untitled pre-header content and a new '## The Need for Multimodal AI' section; both are treated together as the counterpart to the expected section. Combined, they cover the recap of previous lessons, the transition, why multimodal matters, and two of the expected section's three specific limitation examples (financial reports, medical scans/X-rays) -- building sketches is the one dropped, which is within the single-item tolerance given the other two survive. Notably, this is also the first generation for this course to explicitly name both of the guideline's required real-world use cases (image captioning and object detection) directly in the introduction.

Limitations of Traditional Document Processing:
**1:** Both sections cover the same core argument, the same pipeline steps, and the same rigid/fragile/costly characterization with a concrete accuracy statistic.

Foundations of Multimodal LLMs:
**1:** Unlike the previous generation for this preset, every element of the expected section is now present: the two architectures, the patch/tokenization parallel, contrastive learning, six of the expected section's seven named current models (Llama 4, Gemma 2, Qwen3, GPT-5, Gemini 2.5, Claude -- only DeepSeek is missing, which does not undermine the open/closed-source dichotomy the section demonstrates), the Hybrid Approaches trade-off category, the paragraph on extending the architecture to other modalities via additional encoders, and the diffusion-model distinction. No expected idea is missing this time.

Applying Multimodal LLMs to Images and PDFs:
**1:** All core steps are present with real code: raw bytes, Base64, public URL, object detection with a Pydantic-referenced schema, PDF processing, and object detection on PDF pages. The expected section's multi-image comparison demonstration (scaling the raw-bytes caption example to compare two images) is not reproduced -- only single-image captioning is shown -- but this is a specific extension of the raw-bytes concept rather than a wholly separate idea, and the core raw-bytes concept itself is demonstrated, so this is treated as a minor, defensible compression rather than a missing substantive idea.

Foundations of Multimodal RAG:
**0:** The generic architecture, ColPali's OCR-bypassing role, and the bag-of-embeddings representation are present, and the MaxSim/scaling discussion is unusually thorough (see depth_enhancement). However, as with the previous generation for this preset, the expected section's specific backbone identification (PaliGemma-3B with a SigLIP vision encoder) is never named. Scored the same way as that same omission was scored previously, independent of the enhancement content around it.

Implementing Multimodal RAG for Images, PDFs, and Text:
**0:** The mini-project framing, the image-description workaround (naming Voyage AI, Cohere Embed, and CLIP-based open-source models), the image-grid display, and the indexing/search pseudocode are all present. However, only the transformer-architecture query (demonstrating PDF-page retrieval) is run within this section; the complementary kitten/robot query demonstrating standard-image retrieval is not run here (the kitten/robot image appears earlier only as the object-detection example in the previous section). Since the section's stated scope is 'Images, PDFs, and Text,' running only one of the two within-section demonstrations is the same category of gap scored in previous generations for this course.

Building Multimodal AI Agents:
**1:** The section explicitly enumerates three ways to add multimodal capability to agents (native multimodal inputs/outputs, multimodal retrieval tools, and other tools for external resources like PDFs, screenshots, or audio files), closely matching the expected section's own framing before narrowing into the RAG-tool implementation. The tool definition, agent-building code, test question, and final answer are all present, and the closing line explicitly recaps the combined skills (structured outputs, tools, ReAct, RAG, multimodal), matching the expected section's own closing recap.

Conclusion:
**1:** Both sections wrap up Part 1 and transition to the Part 2 capstone. As with every previous generation for this course, the generated section recaps the OCR-to-native-processing shift rather than the expected section's specific list of combined techniques; this is treated as an acceptable variation in wrap-up framing, and the capstone preview itself matches the expected section closely.

References:
**1:** Both sections contain a numbered list of references serving the same bibliographic purpose.
